subsection: 5. Strong vs weak, concentrated vs dilute

points: A strong acid is completely dissociated (ionised) into ions in water, shown with a single arrow: HCl(aq) → H⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq).
Strong acids include hydrochloric acid (HCl), nitric acid (HNO₃) and sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄).
A weak acid is only slightly dissociated in water: most molecules stay undissociated and an equilibrium is set up, e.g. CH₃COOH(aq) ⇌ CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq).
Weak acids include ethanoic acid (vinegar), citric acid, carbonic acid (CO₂ in water) and most organic acids.
A strong base is completely dissociated in water, e.g. sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide: NaOH(aq) → Na⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq).
A weak base reacts only slightly with water to produce hydroxide ions, e.g. ammonia: NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq).

notes.b: Concentration describes how much acid or base is present; strength describes how far it dissociates. The two are separate properties.
points: Concentration is the amount of acid or base dissolved per litre of solution, measured in mol L⁻¹.
A concentrated acid has a large amount of acid per litre, e.g. 10 M HCl; a dilute acid has a small amount per litre, e.g. 0.1 M HCl.
A dilute strong acid, e.g. 0.01 M HCl, is still fully dissociated.
A concentrated weak acid, e.g. glacial ethanoic acid, is still only slightly dissociated.

notes.h: Evidence that ethanoic acid is weaker than hydrochloric acid
notes.b: Compare 0.1 M hydrochloric acid with 0.1 M ethanoic acid, which have the same concentration.
points: pH: 0.1 M hydrochloric acid has a pH of 1.0, while 0.1 M ethanoic acid has a pH of about 2.9, because it produces far fewer H⁺ ions.
Ethanoic acid has an acid dissociation constant (Ka) of 1.8 × 10⁻⁵, a small value showing that it is only slightly dissociated.
Rate of reaction: magnesium ribbon fizzes much faster in 0.1 M hydrochloric acid than in 0.1 M ethanoic acid, because hydrogen ions are present at a higher concentration.
Conductivity: 0.1 M hydrochloric acid conducts electricity much better than 0.1 M ethanoic acid, because it contains more ions.

Equal volumes of the two acids at the same concentration neutralise the same amount of sodium hydroxide and give the same total volume of hydrogen with excess magnesium, because the weak acid's equilibrium shifts to release more H⁺ as H⁺ is used up.
Safety: concentrated acids and alkalis are corrosive, so wear goggles and gloves; dilute an acid by adding it to water.

keyTerms.definition: An acid that is completely dissociated into ions in water.
An acid that is only slightly dissociated in water, setting up an equilibrium with its ions.
A base that is completely dissociated in water.
A base that reacts only slightly with water to produce hydroxide ions.
The splitting of a compound into ions when it dissolves in water.
The amount of acid or base dissolved per litre of solution, measured in mol L⁻¹.
An acid with a large amount of acid dissolved per litre, e.g. 10 M HCl.
An acid with a small amount of acid dissolved per litre, e.g. 0.1 M HCl.
Able to destroy or burn skin and other materials, as concentrated acids and alkalis are.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between a strong acid and a weak acid, and between a concentrated acid and a dilute acid, giving an example of each.
questions.model: A strong acid is completely dissociated into ions in water, e.g. hydrochloric acid: HCl(aq) → H⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq). A weak acid is only slightly dissociated in water and sets up an equilibrium, e.g. ethanoic acid: CH₃COOH(aq) ⇌ CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq). A concentrated acid has a large amount of acid per litre, e.g. 10 M HCl; a dilute acid has a small amount per litre, e.g. 0.1 M HCl. Strength and concentration are independent: a dilute acid can be strong, and a concentrated acid can be weak.

questions.prompt: Describe two experiments that would show that 0.1 M ethanoic acid is a weaker acid than 0.1 M hydrochloric acid, and explain why equal volumes of the two acids need the same volume of sodium hydroxide to neutralise them.
questions.model: Experiment 1: measure the pH of each acid. 0.1 M hydrochloric acid has a pH of 1.0, while 0.1 M ethanoic acid has a pH of about 2.9, showing that ethanoic acid produces fewer H⁺ ions. Experiment 2: add magnesium ribbon to equal volumes of each acid. The ribbon fizzes much faster in hydrochloric acid, showing that it has a higher concentration of H⁺ ions. Equal volumes of the two acids at the same concentration contain the same amount of acid, so they need the same volume of sodium hydroxide to neutralise them. The weak acid's equilibrium shifts to release more H⁺ as H⁺ is used up, so all of its acid is neutralised.
